and in what I have tested, he was never a liar.

Three nights, each night he would say:
"A messenger from Luayy ibn Ghalib has come to you."

So I hitched up my izar above my calves,
and the swift, strong she-camel carried me through the desert plains.

I bear witness that Allah, there is no lord but Him,
and that you are trusted over every unseen matter.

And that you are the nearest of the messengers in intercession
to Allah, O son of the most noble and the best.

So command us with what comes to you, O best of messengers,
even if what has come is the greying of the forelocks.

Be for me an intercessor on the day when no one has intercession
besides you, to suffice for Sawad ibn Qarib.

He said: The Prophet ﷺ laughed until his back teeth were visible, and said to me: "You have prospered, O Sawad!" Then Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: "Does your companion still come to you now?" He said: "Since I recited the Qur'an, he has not come to me, and the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is a fine replacement for the jinn." Then al-Bayhaqi transmitted it through two other routes. The words of Ibn Kathir end here.

It has been related by Imam al-Mawardi in (A'lam al-Nubuwwah) together with similar reports, in the sixteenth chapter, on the calls of the jinn. Then he said: Even if these calls are khabar al-ahad (solitary reports) from one whose person is not seen and whose testimony is not decisive, their departure from the ordinary habit is a warning, and their effect on souls is a glad tiding, and the listeners have accepted them. The acceptance of reports confirms their soundness and supports their proof. If it is said: If the calls of the jinn are among the signs of prophethood, [p. 5364] then it could also be a proof for the validity of kahanah (soothsaying), then there are two answers to this:

The first: the signs of prophethood are other than these; rather, these are among its heralds, and he distinguished between a sign (dalalah) and a glad tiding (bisharah) by way of information.

The second: soothsaying concerns the hidden, while glad tidings concern a specific matter; the observed is known, and the unseen is imagined. The words of al-Mawardi end here.

The second point of caution:

Al-Mawardi said: Regarding the turning away (sarf) of the jinn mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: they were turned away from eavesdropping on the heaven by the hurling of shooting stars, and they were not turned away from it after Jesus except after the sending of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So they said: "This event in the heaven is only for an event on the earth," and they imagined in it the renewal of prophethood. So they traversed the earth until they came upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the valley of Makkah, as he was heading to Ukaz and was performing the dawn prayer. They listened to the Qur'an, saw how he prayed, and his companions followed him. Thus they knew that this was for this event, and they were turned away from eavesdropping by the hurling of meteors. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.

I say: According to this view, the (ila) in (ilayka) means the same as the lam of causation. It is mentioned in (al-Mughni) that it may come synonymous with the lam, as in: "and the matter is to you." But this is strained and remote, because it is far from what the context of the rest of the verse requires.

Then al-Mawardi said: [p. 5365] Ikrimah related that the surah he used to recite was ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-Alaq: 1]. I say: It will come later, traced back to the Prophet through Jabir, that it was Surat al-Rahman.

Then al-Mawardi said:

The second interpretation: they were turned away from their lands by divine guidance, through Allah's grace, until they came to the Prophet of Allah in the valley of Nakhlah. Then Jibril descended to him with this verse, informed him of the coming of the jinn, and commanded him to go out to them. He went out with Ibn Masud, until he came to al-Hajun. Ibn Masud said: "He drew a line for me and said: Do not cross it."

According to the first interpretation, he did not know of them until they came to him. According to the second interpretation, Jibril informed him before their coming. The scholars differed over whether he saw them and recited to them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not see them and did not recite to them; rather, they heard his recitation when they passed by him while he was praying. Ibn Masud related that he saw them and recited the Qur'an to them.

I say: What Ibn Kathir has mentioned earlier is sufficient.

Then al-Mawardi said: Regarding His saying ﴿When they attended it, they said: Be silent﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: when they attended his recitation of the Qur'an, they said: "Be silent to listen to it."

The second: when they attended the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they said: "Be silent to listen to his words." The words of al-Mawardi end here.

Ibn Kathir said: This, that is their saying "Be silent," is a mark of good manners on their part. Al-Bayhaqi related from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Surat al-Rahman until he finished it, then said: 'Why do I see you silent? The jinn were better than you in response. Every time I recited to them this verse: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾, they would say: "Nor do we deny any of Your favours, our Lord; to You be praise."'" It was also transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, who said: "We do not know it except from the hadith of al-Walid ibn Muslim from Zuhayr."

The third point: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31] indicates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent generally to both mankind and the jinn.

[p. 5366] Ibn Kathir said: Because he called the jinn to Allah, and recited to them the surah in which there is address to both groups, their obligations, promises, and threats, and that is Surat al-Rahman. This is why He said: ﴿Respond to the caller of Allah and believe in Him﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. Al-Mawardi said: The scholars have not disagreed that it is permissible for Allah to send a messenger from mankind to them, but they differed over the permissibility of a messenger from among them. Some permitted it, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130], while others forbade it. This is the view of those who made them the offspring of Iblis, and they interpreted His saying ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130] as referring to those who, when they heard the Qur'an, turned back to their people as warners. The words of al-Mawardi end here.

I say: A parallel to this is the naming of the messengers of Jesus, peace be upon him, as "messengers" in the verse ﴿When We sent to them two﴾ [Ya-Sin: 14].

The fourth point: Those scholars who held that believing jinn do not enter Paradise have used as evidence His saying ﴿He will forgive you of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. They said: the reward of their righteous ones is only that they be protected from the punishment of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection; for if they had a reward for faith higher than this, it would have been mentioned.

Al-Mawardi said: As for their disbelievers, they will enter the Fire. As for their believers, they differed over whether they enter Paradise as a reward for their faith. Al-Dahhak said: "Whoever permits that their messengers were from among them, they will enter Paradise." Sufyan related from Layth that they will be rewarded for faith by being protected from the Fire, and then it will be said to them: "Be dust like the beasts." The words of al-Mawardi end here.

The truth, as Ibn Kathir said, is that their believer is like the believer among mankind; they enter Paradise, as is the view of a group of the early generations (al-salaf). Some of them have used as evidence for this His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾ [al-Rahman: 74]. But there is room for scrutiny in this argument. A better proof is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 47]. He, the Exalted, has bestowed His favour upon both the two weighty groups by making the reward of their good-doers Paradise. The jinn responded to this verse with verbal gratitude more eloquently than mankind, saying: "Nor do we deny any of Your favours, our Lord; to You be praise." So He, the Exalted, would not bestow favour upon them with a reward that they do not attain.

Also, if He repays their disbelievers with the Fire, which is a station of justice, then all the more He repays their believers with Paradise, which is a station of grace, by way of a stronger and more fitting argument. Among what also indicates the generality of this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging﴾ [al-Kahf: 107], and what resembles that of verses. What they have mentioned here of reward for faith, namely the expiation of sins and protection from the painful punishment, necessarily entails entering Paradise, because in the Hereafter there is nothing but Paradise or the Fire. Whoever is protected from the Fire enters Paradise without doubt. No explicit text or apparent evidence from the Lawgiver has reached us stating that believing jinn do not enter Paradise even if they are protected from the Fire; and if it were authentic, we would adopt it. And Allah knows best. Here is Noah, peace be upon him, saying to his people: ﴿He will forgive you of your sins and delay you until a specified term﴾ [Nuh: 4]. There is no disagreement that the believers among his people are in Paradise; so likewise these. Strange views have been reported about them. From Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: they will not enter the center of Paradise, but will be around its outskirts, its surroundings, and its edges.

Some people claimed that in Paradise the children of Adam will see them, while they will not see the children of Adam, the reverse of their state in the worldly abode. Some people said: they do not eat or drink in Paradise, but they are inspired with glorification, praise, and sanctification in place of food and drink, like the angels, because they are of their kind. All these views are open to scrutiny and have no proof. The words of al-Mawardi end here.

The fifth point: It has been said: the secret of the partial (tab'id) in His saying ﴿of your sins﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31] is that there is a punishment that is not forgiven by faith, such as the sins of injustice (al-mazalim), that is, the rights of people. But there is room for scrutiny in this, because if a combatant (harbi) plunders protected property and sheds sanctified blood, and then his Islam is good, Islam erases the sin of what came before him without any problem. [p. 5368] It is said: He did not promise forgiveness to the disbeliever on condition of faith in the Book of Allah except in a partial form. The secret of this is that the station of the disbeliever is constriction (qabd), not expansion (bast), and therefore his hope is not expanded as it is in the case of the believer. This was related by al-Nasir.

The sixth point: Ibn Kathir said: In their claim to their people they combined encouragement and warning, and for this reason it had an effect on many of them, and they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in delegations, delegation after delegation, as has already been explained.

The seventh point: Al-Mawardi said: The jinn belong to the speaking, discerning world. They eat, marry, reproduce, and die. Their persons are veiled from sight, although they are distinguished by actions and traces; but Allah singles out whom He wills to see them. Mankind came to know them from the divine books and from what they imagined of their hidden traces.

Al-Qashani said: The jinn are earthly souls embodied in subtle bodies composed of subtle elements. The sages of Persia named them "the suspended forms." Because they are earthly, embodied in elemental bodies, and share this with mankind, both are called "the two weighty ones" (al-thaqalan). Just as it was possible for people to challenge with the Qur'an, it was possible for them too, and the reports of them from the verifiers and others are more than can be counted, and too clear to accept interpretation. The words of al-Qashani end here.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 46, verses 29–32 (part 1 of 2)**

On the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[29–32] ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an. When they attended it, they said, "Be silent." And when it was concluded, they returned to their people as warners.﴾ ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path."﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30] ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31] ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah will not escape [Allah] on earth, and he will have no protectors besides Him. Those are in clear error.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 32]

﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾, meaning: We directed them to you and brought them towards you. ﴿Listening to the Qur'an. When they attended it, they said, "Be silent"﴾, meaning: so that reflection and contemplation could be completed. ﴿And when it was concluded﴾, meaning: when he had finished reciting it, and its effect upon them was complete, they wished to convey its effect [to others], therefore: ﴿they returned﴾, meaning: they went back ﴿to their people as warners﴾, meaning: warning them against the error in which they were. ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], meaning: one whose greatness is agreed upon. That is: and we have known its truthfulness because it is ﴿confirming what came before it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], meaning: of all these earlier books, and it has been given preference over them in that it ﴿guides to the truth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], meaning: to knowledge of realities, ﴿and to a straight path﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], meaning: without crookedness, which is Islam.

[p. 5358] Ibn Kathir said: That is, it guides to the truth in belief and in reports, and to a straight path in deeds. The Qur'an comprises two things: information (khabar) and command (talab). Its information is truthful, and its command is just, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115]. He, Exalted is He, also said: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth﴾ [al-Fath: 28]. So guidance is beneficial knowledge, and the religion of truth is righteous action. Thus the jinn said: ﴿guides to the truth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30] in matters of belief, and ﴿to a straight path﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], that is, in practical matters. ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31], that is, the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, in what he calls you to of obedience to Allah. ﴿And believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah will not escape [Allah] on earth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 32], that is, he cannot escape his Lord by fleeing when He wills to punish him, for he is within His grasp and authority wherever he turns. ﴿And he will have no protectors besides Him﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 32], that is, helpers who would defend him against Allah if He punishes him. ﴿Those are in clear error﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 32], that is, they have taken a path other than uprightness.

Remarks:

The first: Imam Muslim narrated from Alqamah, who said: "I asked Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Was anyone among you present with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the night of the jinn?' He said: 'No. But we were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ one night and we lost him. We searched for him in the valleys and the mountain paths, and it was said: he has been carried off, or he has been seized! He said: So we spent the worst night any people have spent. When we rose in the morning, behold, he came from the direction of Hira'. We said: O Messenger of Allah! We lost you, we searched for you and did not find you, so we spent the worst night any people have spent. He said: "The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went with them and recited the Qur'an to them." He said: Then he set out with us and showed us their traces.'"

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The jinn used to eavesdrop on the revelation [wahy], and they would hear a word and add ten to it. What they heard was true, and what they added was false. Before that, shooting stars were not hurled at them. But when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent, whenever one of them went to his seat [in the heavens] he would be struck by a flaming meteor that burned whatever it hit. So they complained of this to Iblis, who said: 'This is nothing but some new matter that has occurred.' He then dispatched his troops, and found the Prophet ﷺ praying between two hills of a palm grove. They came to him and informed him, and he said: 'This is the new event that has happened on earth.'" At-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa'i narrated it in the books of tafsir of their Sunan. Likewise al-Hasan al-Basri said: he ﷺ was not aware of their matter until Allah revealed to him the news of them.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi the story of the Prophet's ﷺ departure to Ta'if, his calling them to Allah, the Most High, and their refusal of him. He related the story at length, then said: When he turned away from them, he spent the night at Nakhla, and he recited the Qur'an that night, and the jinn of Nasibin heard it. Ibn Kathir said: This is authentic, but his statement that the jinn's listening took place that night is open to question, for the jinn's listening was at the beginning of the revelation, as the hadith of Ibn Abbas mentioned above indicates. His departure to Ta'if was after the death of his uncle, and that was one or two years before the Hijrah, as Ibn Ishaq and others have established.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "They descended upon the Prophet ﷺ while he was reciting the Qur'an in the hollow of Nakhla. When they heard it, they said: 'Be silent!' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾, the verse." Ibn Kathir said: This, together with the first report from Ibn Abbas, may he be pleased with them both, implies that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was not aware of their presence on this occasion; they only listened to his recitation and then returned to their people. Afterwards they came to him in successive delegations, one group after another and one company after another.

[p. 5360] As for what al-Bukhari and Muslim both narrated from Ma'n ibn Abd al-Rahman, who said: "I heard my father say: I asked Masruq: 'Who informed the Prophet ﷺ on the night they listened to the Qur'an?' He said: 'Your father, that is Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, told me that a tree informed him of them.'" It is possible that this refers to the first occasion, and that it is an affirmation which takes precedence over Ibn Abbas's negation. It is also possible that it refers to the first occasion, but that he was not aware of them while they were listening, until the tree informed him of their gathering. And it is possible that this refers to one of the later occasions. And Allah knows best.

The hafiz al-Bayhaqi said: What Ibn Abbas related is only the first time the jinn heard the recitation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and learned of his condition; at that time he did not recite to them and did not see them. Then after that, the caller of the jinn came to him, and he recited the Qur'an to them and called them to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated.

Ibn Kathir then said: As for Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, he was not with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during his address to the jinn and his calling them, but was far from him, and no one went out with the Prophet ﷺ except him. Even so, he did not witness the address itself. This is al-Bayhaqi's view. It is possible that on the first occasion he went out to them, Ibn Mas'ud and others were not with him ﷺ, as the apparent context of the first narration through Imam Muslim indicates. Then afterwards he went out with him on another night, and Allah knows best, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in his tafsir on ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1] from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Abd al-Aziz ibn Umar said: As for the jinn who met him at Nakhla, they were the jinn of Nineveh, and as for the jinn who met him in Makkah, they were the jinn of Nasibin.

Al-Bayhaqi interpreted the statement "we spent the worst night" as referring to someone other than Ibn Mas'ud, namely someone who was not aware of the Prophet's ﷺ going out to the jinn. This is possible, though a remote interpretation. [p. 5361] In sum, there has been transmitted what indicates that this occurred repeatedly. It has also been transmitted from Ibn Abbas, through a sound chain cited by Ibn Jarir on this verse, something other than what was transmitted from him earlier: he said: They were seven men from the people of Nasibin, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them messengers to their people. This indicates that he narrated both accounts. Abu Hamzah al-Thumali mentioned that this tribe of the jinn were the most numerous of the jinn and the noblest in lineage. It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud that they were nine. It is said that they were fifteen, it is reported as sixty, and it is reported as three hundred. From Ikrimah it is reported that they were twelve thousand. Ibn Kathir said: Perhaps this difference is evidence of their repeated delegations to him ﷺ.

Among what indicates this is what al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih: that Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "I never heard Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, say about anything: 'I think it is thus,' except that it turned out as he thought. While Umar ibn al-Khattab was sitting, a handsome man passed by him, and he said: 'My assumption has been mistaken, or this man is upon his religion of the Jahiliyyah, or he was their soothsayer. Bring the man to me.' He was summoned, and [Umar] said to him what he had said. [The man] said: 'I have never seen a Muslim man confronted with the like of what you have just done today.' [Umar] said: 'I adjure you to tell me [the truth]!'

He said: 'I was their soothsayer in the Jahiliyyah.' [Umar] said: 'What is the most astonishing thing your jinn companion (ra'iy) brought you?' He said: 'One day while I was in the market, she came to me, and I could see fear in her. She said: Have you not seen the jinn and their abasement, their despair after their reversal, and their clinging to the mares and their saddle-cloths?' Umar said: 'She spoke the truth! While I was sleeping near their idols, a man came with a calf and slaughtered it, and a shouter cried out with it, a shout the like of which I had never heard, saying: "O Jalih! A successful matter, an eloquent man, saying: There is no god but Allah!" The people leapt up, and I said: I will not leave until I know what lies behind this. Then he called out again: "O Jalih! A successful matter, an eloquent man, saying: There is no god but Allah!" I got up, and we had not yet gone far before it was said: This is a Prophet.'" This is the wording of al-Bukhari. Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it with similar wording from the hadith of Ibn Wahb.

Then he said: The apparent meaning of this report gives the impression that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, himself heard the shouter crying out from the calf that had been slaughtered. [p. 5362] Indeed, this is explicit in a weak report from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. But the rest of the reports indicate that it was this soothsayer who reported it from his own seeing and hearing. And Allah knows best.

This man was Sawad ibn Qarib. Al-Bayhaqi said: Sawad ibn Qarib is likely to be the soothsayer whose name is not mentioned in the sound hadith. Then he narrated with his chain from al-Bara', who said: "While Umar ibn al-Khattab was delivering a sermon to the people from the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said: 'O people! Is Sawad ibn Qarib among you?' No one answered him that year. When the following year came, he said: 'O people! Is Sawad ibn Qarib among you?' I said: 'O Commander of the Faithful! Who is Sawad ibn Qarib?' Umar said to him: 'Sawad ibn Qarib's beginning in Islam was something astonishing!' He said: While we were in this state, Sawad ibn Qarib appeared. Umar said to him: 'O Sawad! Tell us how your beginning in Islam came about.' Sawad said: 'I was staying in India, and I had a companion (ra'iy) from among the jinn.' He said: 'One night while I was sleeping, it came to me in my dream and said: Rise, understand and reflect, if you are able to reflect! A messenger has been sent from Lu'ayy ibn Ghalib.' Then it began to recite:

I marvelled at the jinn and their pursuit, and their driving of camels with their saddle-cloths.
They yearn towards Makkah seeking guidance; the best of the jinn are not like their wretched ones.
So rise to the chosen one of Hashim, and let your eyes be turned towards its head.

He said: Then it roused me and frightened me and said: 'O Sawad ibn Qarib! Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has sent a prophet, so rise towards him and you will be guided and rightly directed.' When it was the second night, it came to me, roused me, and then began to recite:

I marvelled at the jinn and their pursuit, and their driving of camels by their saddle-pads.
They yearn towards Makkah seeking guidance; their two forefeet are not like their tails.
So rise to the chosen one of Hashim, and let your eyes be turned towards its [forehead].

When it was the third night, it came to me, roused me, and then said:

I marvelled at the jinn and their knowledge [of the unseen], and their driving of camels by their packs.
They yearn towards Makkah seeking guidance; those with evil are not like the good among them.
So rise to the chosen one of Hashim; the believing jinn are not like their unbelievers.

[p. 5363] He said: When he heard it repeated night after night, the love of Islam entered my heart, by the decree of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to the extent that Allah willed. He said: I went to my saddlebag, tied it tightly on my mount, and did not untie one cord or tie another until I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He was in Madinah, meaning Makkah, and the people around him were like the mane of a horse. When the Prophet ﷺ saw me, he said: "Welcome to you, O Sawad ibn Qarib. We know what has brought you." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have composed a poem. Let me recite it to you." He ﷺ said: "Say it, O Sawad." So I said:

My companion came to me after a night and a sleep,
and in what I have tested, he was never a liar.

Three nights, each night he would say:
"A messenger from Luayy ibn Ghalib has come to you."

So I hitched up my izar above my calves,
and the swift, strong she-camel carried me through the desert plains.

I bear witness that Allah, there is no lord but Him,
and that you are trusted over every unseen matter.

And that you are the nearest of the messengers in intercession
to Allah, O son of the most noble and the best.

So command us with what comes to you, O best of messengers,
even if what has come is the greying of the forelocks.

Be for me an intercessor on the day when no one has intercession
besides you, to suffice for Sawad ibn Qarib.

He said: The Prophet ﷺ laughed until his back teeth were visible, and said to me: "You have prospered, O Sawad!" Then Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: "Does your companion still come to you now?" He said: "Since I recited the Qur'an, he has not come to me, and the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is a fine replacement for the jinn." Then al-Bayhaqi transmitted it through two other routes. The words of Ibn Kathir end here.

It has been related by Imam al-Mawardi in (A'lam al-Nubuwwah) together with similar reports, in the sixteenth chapter, on the calls of the jinn. Then he said: Even if these calls are khabar al-ahad (solitary reports) from one whose person is not seen and whose testimony is not decisive, their departure from the ordinary habit is a warning, and their effect on souls is a glad tiding, and the listeners have accepted them. The acceptance of reports confirms their soundness and supports their proof. If it is said: If the calls of the jinn are among the signs of prophethood, [p. 5364] then it could also be a proof for the validity of kahanah (soothsaying), then there are two answers to this:

The first: the signs of prophethood are other than these; rather, these are among its heralds, and he distinguished between a sign (dalalah) and a glad tiding (bisharah) by way of information.

The second: soothsaying concerns the hidden, while glad tidings concern a specific matter; the observed is known, and the unseen is imagined. The words of al-Mawardi end here.

The second point of caution:

Al-Mawardi said: Regarding the turning away (sarf) of the jinn mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: they were turned away from eavesdropping on the heaven by the hurling of shooting stars, and they were not turned away from it after Jesus except after the sending of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So they said: "This event in the heaven is only for an event on the earth," and they imagined in it the renewal of prophethood. So they traversed the earth until they came upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the valley of Makkah, as he was heading to Ukaz and was performing the dawn prayer. They listened to the Qur'an, saw how he prayed, and his companions followed him. Thus they knew that this was for this event, and they were turned away from eavesdropping by the hurling of meteors. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.

I say: According to this view, the (ila) in (ilayka) means the same as the lam of causation. It is mentioned in (al-Mughni) that it may come synonymous with the lam, as in: "and the matter is to you." But this is strained and remote, because it is far from what the context of the rest of the verse requires.

Then al-Mawardi said: [p. 5365] Ikrimah related that the surah he used to recite was ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-Alaq: 1]. I say: It will come later, traced back to the Prophet through Jabir, that it was Surat al-Rahman.

Then al-Mawardi said:

The second interpretation: they were turned away from their lands by divine guidance, through Allah's grace, until they came to the Prophet of Allah in the valley of Nakhlah. Then Jibril descended to him with this verse, informed him of the coming of the jinn, and commanded him to go out to them. He went out with Ibn Masud, until he came to al-Hajun. Ibn Masud said: "He drew a line for me and said: Do not cross it."

According to the first interpretation, he did not know of them until they came to him. According to the second interpretation, Jibril informed him before their coming. The scholars differed over whether he saw them and recited to them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not see them and did not recite to them; rather, they heard his recitation when they passed by him while he was praying. Ibn Masud related that he saw them and recited the Qur'an to them.

I say: What Ibn Kathir has mentioned earlier is sufficient.

Then al-Mawardi said: Regarding His saying ﴿When they attended it, they said: Be silent﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: when they attended his recitation of the Qur'an, they said: "Be silent to listen to it."

The second: when they attended the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they said: "Be silent to listen to his words." The words of al-Mawardi end here.

Ibn Kathir said: This, that is their saying "Be silent," is a mark of good manners on their part. Al-Bayhaqi related from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Surat al-Rahman until he finished it, then said: 'Why do I see you silent? The jinn were better than you in response. Every time I recited to them this verse: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾, they would say: "Nor do we deny any of Your favours, our Lord; to You be praise."'" It was also transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, who said: "We do not know it except from the hadith of al-Walid ibn Muslim from Zuhayr."

The third point: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31] indicates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent generally to both mankind and the jinn.

[p. 5366] Ibn Kathir said: Because he called the jinn to Allah, and recited to them the surah in which there is address to both groups, their obligations, promises, and threats, and that is Surat al-Rahman. This is why He said: ﴿Respond to the caller of Allah and believe in Him﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. Al-Mawardi said: The scholars have not disagreed that it is permissible for Allah to send a messenger from mankind to them, but they differed over the permissibility of a messenger from among them. Some permitted it, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130], while others forbade it. This is the view of those who made them the offspring of Iblis, and they interpreted His saying ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130] as referring to those who, when they heard the Qur'an, turned back to their people as warners. The words of al-Mawardi end here.

I say: A parallel to this is the naming of the messengers of Jesus, peace be upon him, as "messengers" in the verse ﴿When We sent to them two﴾ [Ya-Sin: 14].

The fourth point: Those scholars who held that believing jinn do not enter Paradise have used as evidence His saying ﴿He will forgive you of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. They said: the reward of their righteous ones is only that they be protected from the punishment of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection; for if they had a reward for faith higher than this, it would have been mentioned.

Al-Mawardi said: As for their disbelievers, they will enter the Fire. As for their believers, they differed over whether they enter Paradise as a reward for their faith. Al-Dahhak said: "Whoever permits that their messengers were from among them, they will enter Paradise." Sufyan related from Layth that they will be rewarded for faith by being protected from the Fire, and then it will be said to them: "Be dust like the beasts." The words of al-Mawardi end here.

The truth, as Ibn Kathir said, is that their believer is like the believer among mankind; they enter Paradise, as is the view of a group of the early generations (al-salaf). Some of them have used as evidence for this His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾ [al-Rahman: 74]. But there is room for scrutiny in this argument. A better proof is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 47]. He, the Exalted, has bestowed His favour upon both the two weighty groups by making the reward of their good-doers Paradise. The jinn responded to this verse with verbal gratitude more eloquently than mankind, saying: "Nor do we deny any of Your favours, our Lord; to You be praise." So He, the Exalted, would not bestow favour upon them with a reward that they do not attain.

Also, if He repays their disbelievers with the Fire, which is a station of justice, then all the more He repays their believers with Paradise, which is a station of grace, by way of a stronger and more fitting argument. Among what also indicates the generality of this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging﴾ [al-Kahf: 107], and what resembles that of verses. What they have mentioned here of reward for faith, namely the expiation of sins and protection from the painful punishment, necessarily entails entering Paradise, because in the Hereafter there is nothing but Paradise or the Fire. Whoever is protected from the Fire enters Paradise without doubt. No explicit text or apparent evidence from the Lawgiver has reached us stating that believing jinn do not enter Paradise even if they are protected from the Fire; and if it were authentic, we would adopt it. And Allah knows best. Here is Noah, peace be upon him, saying to his people: ﴿He will forgive you of your sins and delay you until a specified term﴾ [Nuh: 4]. There is no disagreement that the believers among his people are in Paradise; so likewise these. Strange views have been reported about them. From Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: they will not enter the center of Paradise, but will be around its outskirts, its surroundings, and its edges.

Some people claimed that in Paradise the children of Adam will see them, while they will not see the children of Adam, the reverse of their state in the worldly abode. Some people said: they do not eat or drink in Paradise, but they are inspired with glorification, praise, and sanctification in place of food and drink, like the angels, because they are of their kind. All these views are open to scrutiny and have no proof. The words of al-Mawardi end here.

The fifth point: It has been said: the secret of the partial (tab'id) in His saying ﴿of your sins﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31] is that there is a punishment that is not forgiven by faith, such as the sins of injustice (al-mazalim), that is, the rights of people. But there is room for scrutiny in this, because if a combatant (harbi) plunders protected property and sheds sanctified blood, and then his Islam is good, Islam erases the sin of what came before him without any problem. [p. 5368] It is said: He did not promise forgiveness to the disbeliever on condition of faith in the Book of Allah except in a partial form. The secret of this is that the station of the disbeliever is constriction (qabd), not expansion (bast), and therefore his hope is not expanded as it is in the case of the believer. This was related by al-Nasir.

The sixth point: Ibn Kathir said: In their claim to their people they combined encouragement and warning, and for this reason it had an effect on many of them, and they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in delegations, delegation after delegation, as has already been explained.

The seventh point: Al-Mawardi said: The jinn belong to the speaking, discerning world. They eat, marry, reproduce, and die. Their persons are veiled from sight, although they are distinguished by actions and traces; but Allah singles out whom He wills to see them. Mankind came to know them from the divine books and from what they imagined of their hidden traces.

Al-Qashani said: The jinn are earthly souls embodied in subtle bodies composed of subtle elements. The sages of Persia named them "the suspended forms." Because they are earthly, embodied in elemental bodies, and share this with mankind, both are called "the two weighty ones" (al-thaqalan). Just as it was possible for people to challenge with the Qur'an, it was possible for them too, and the reports of them from the verifiers and others are more than can be counted, and too clear to accept interpretation. The words of al-Qashani end here.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 46, verses 29–32 (part 1 of 2)**

On the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[29–32] ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an. When they attended it, they said, "Be silent." And when it was concluded, they returned to their people as warners.﴾ ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path."﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30] ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31] ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah will not escape [Allah] on earth, and he will have no protectors besides Him. Those are in clear error.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 32]

﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾, meaning: We directed them to you and brought them towards you. ﴿Listening to the Qur'an. When they attended it, they said, "Be silent"﴾, meaning: so that reflection and contemplation could be completed. ﴿And when it was concluded﴾, meaning: when he had finished reciting it, and its effect upon them was complete, they wished to convey its effect [to others], therefore: ﴿they returned﴾, meaning: they went back ﴿to their people as warners﴾, meaning: warning them against the error in which they were. ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], meaning: one whose greatness is agreed upon. That is: and we have known its truthfulness because it is ﴿confirming what came before it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], meaning: of all these earlier books, and it has been given preference over them in that it ﴿guides to the truth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], meaning: to knowledge of realities, ﴿and to a straight path﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], meaning: without crookedness, which is Islam.

[p. 5358] Ibn Kathir said: That is, it guides to the truth in belief and in reports, and to a straight path in deeds. The Qur'an comprises two things: information (khabar) and command (talab). Its information is truthful, and its command is just, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am: 115]. He, Exalted is He, also said: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth﴾ [al-Fath: 28]. So guidance is beneficial knowledge, and the religion of truth is righteous action. Thus the jinn said: ﴿guides to the truth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30] in matters of belief, and ﴿to a straight path﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], that is, in practical matters. ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31], that is, the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad, in what he calls you to of obedience to Allah. ﴿And believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah will not escape [Allah] on earth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 32], that is, he cannot escape his Lord by fleeing when He wills to punish him, for he is within His grasp and authority wherever he turns. ﴿And he will have no protectors besides Him﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 32], that is, helpers who would defend him against Allah if He punishes him. ﴿Those are in clear error﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 32], that is, they have taken a path other than uprightness.

Remarks:

The first: Imam Muslim narrated from Alqamah, who said: "I asked Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Was anyone among you present with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the night of the jinn?' He said: 'No. But we were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ one night and we lost him. We searched for him in the valleys and the mountain paths, and it was said: he has been carried off, or he has been seized! He said: So we spent the worst night any people have spent. When we rose in the morning, behold, he came from the direction of Hira'. We said: O Messenger of Allah! We lost you, we searched for you and did not find you, so we spent the worst night any people have spent. He said: "The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went with them and recited the Qur'an to them." He said: Then he set out with us and showed us their traces.'"

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The jinn used to eavesdrop on the revelation [wahy], and they would hear a word and add ten to it. What they heard was true, and what they added was false. Before that, shooting stars were not hurled at them. But when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent, whenever one of them went to his seat [in the heavens] he would be struck by a flaming meteor that burned whatever it hit. So they complained of this to Iblis, who said: 'This is nothing but some new matter that has occurred.' He then dispatched his troops, and found the Prophet ﷺ praying between two hills of a palm grove. They came to him and informed him, and he said: 'This is the new event that has happened on earth.'" At-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa'i narrated it in the books of tafsir of their Sunan. Likewise al-Hasan al-Basri said: he ﷺ was not aware of their matter until Allah revealed to him the news of them.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi the story of the Prophet's ﷺ departure to Ta'if, his calling them to Allah, the Most High, and their refusal of him. He related the story at length, then said: When he turned away from them, he spent the night at Nakhla, and he recited the Qur'an that night, and the jinn of Nasibin heard it. Ibn Kathir said: This is authentic, but his statement that the jinn's listening took place that night is open to question, for the jinn's listening was at the beginning of the revelation, as the hadith of Ibn Abbas mentioned above indicates. His departure to Ta'if was after the death of his uncle, and that was one or two years before the Hijrah, as Ibn Ishaq and others have established.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "They descended upon the Prophet ﷺ while he was reciting the Qur'an in the hollow of Nakhla. When they heard it, they said: 'Be silent!' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾, the verse." Ibn Kathir said: This, together with the first report from Ibn Abbas, may he be pleased with them both, implies that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was not aware of their presence on this occasion; they only listened to his recitation and then returned to their people. Afterwards they came to him in successive delegations, one group after another and one company after another.

[p. 5360] As for what al-Bukhari and Muslim both narrated from Ma'n ibn Abd al-Rahman, who said: "I heard my father say: I asked Masruq: 'Who informed the Prophet ﷺ on the night they listened to the Qur'an?' He said: 'Your father, that is Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, told me that a tree informed him of them.'" It is possible that this refers to the first occasion, and that it is an affirmation which takes precedence over Ibn Abbas's negation. It is also possible that it refers to the first occasion, but that he was not aware of them while they were listening, until the tree informed him of their gathering. And it is possible that this refers to one of the later occasions. And Allah knows best.

The hafiz al-Bayhaqi said: What Ibn Abbas related is only the first time the jinn heard the recitation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and learned of his condition; at that time he did not recite to them and did not see them. Then after that, the caller of the jinn came to him, and he recited the Qur'an to them and called them to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated.

Ibn Kathir then said: As for Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, he was not with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during his address to the jinn and his calling them, but was far from him, and no one went out with the Prophet ﷺ except him. Even so, he did not witness the address itself. This is al-Bayhaqi's view. It is possible that on the first occasion he went out to them, Ibn Mas'ud and others were not with him ﷺ, as the apparent context of the first narration through Imam Muslim indicates. Then afterwards he went out with him on another night, and Allah knows best, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in his tafsir on ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾ [al-Jinn: 1] from the hadith of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Abd al-Aziz ibn Umar said: As for the jinn who met him at Nakhla, they were the jinn of Nineveh, and as for the jinn who met him in Makkah, they were the jinn of Nasibin.

Al-Bayhaqi interpreted the statement "we spent the worst night" as referring to someone other than Ibn Mas'ud, namely someone who was not aware of the Prophet's ﷺ going out to the jinn. This is possible, though a remote interpretation. [p. 5361] In sum, there has been transmitted what indicates that this occurred repeatedly. It has also been transmitted from Ibn Abbas, through a sound chain cited by Ibn Jarir on this verse, something other than what was transmitted from him earlier: he said: They were seven men from the people of Nasibin, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them messengers to their people. This indicates that he narrated both accounts. Abu Hamzah al-Thumali mentioned that this tribe of the jinn were the most numerous of the jinn and the noblest in lineage. It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud that they were nine. It is said that they were fifteen, it is reported as sixty, and it is reported as three hundred. From Ikrimah it is reported that they were twelve thousand. Ibn Kathir said: Perhaps this difference is evidence of their repeated delegations to him ﷺ.

Among what indicates this is what al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih: that Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "I never heard Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, say about anything: 'I think it is thus,' except that it turned out as he thought. While Umar ibn al-Khattab was sitting, a handsome man passed by him, and he said: 'My assumption has been mistaken, or this man is upon his religion of the Jahiliyyah, or he was their soothsayer. Bring the man to me.' He was summoned, and [Umar] said to him what he had said. [The man] said: 'I have never seen a Muslim man confronted with the like of what you have just done today.' [Umar] said: 'I adjure you to tell me [the truth]!'

He said: 'I was their soothsayer in the Jahiliyyah.' [Umar] said: 'What is the most astonishing thing your jinn companion (ra'iy) brought you?' He said: 'One day while I was in the market, she came to me, and I could see fear in her. She said: Have you not seen the jinn and their abasement, their despair after their reversal, and their clinging to the mares and their saddle-cloths?' Umar said: 'She spoke the truth! While I was sleeping near their idols, a man came with a calf and slaughtered it, and a shouter cried out with it, a shout the like of which I had never heard, saying: "O Jalih! A successful matter, an eloquent man, saying: There is no god but Allah!" The people leapt up, and I said: I will not leave until I know what lies behind this. Then he called out again: "O Jalih! A successful matter, an eloquent man, saying: There is no god but Allah!" I got up, and we had not yet gone far before it was said: This is a Prophet.'" This is the wording of al-Bukhari. Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it with similar wording from the hadith of Ibn Wahb.

Then he said: The apparent meaning of this report gives the impression that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, himself heard the shouter crying out from the calf that had been slaughtered. [p. 5362] Indeed, this is explicit in a weak report from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. But the rest of the reports indicate that it was this soothsayer who reported it from his own seeing and hearing. And Allah knows best.

This man was Sawad ibn Qarib. Al-Bayhaqi said: Sawad ibn Qarib is likely to be the soothsayer whose name is not mentioned in the sound hadith. Then he narrated with his chain from al-Bara', who said: "While Umar ibn al-Khattab was delivering a sermon to the people from the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said: 'O people! Is Sawad ibn Qarib among you?' No one answered him that year. When the following year came, he said: 'O people! Is Sawad ibn Qarib among you?' I said: 'O Commander of the Faithful! Who is Sawad ibn Qarib?' Umar said to him: 'Sawad ibn Qarib's beginning in Islam was something astonishing!' He said: While we were in this state, Sawad ibn Qarib appeared. Umar said to him: 'O Sawad! Tell us how your beginning in Islam came about.' Sawad said: 'I was staying in India, and I had a companion (ra'iy) from among the jinn.' He said: 'One night while I was sleeping, it came to me in my dream and said: Rise, understand and reflect, if you are able to reflect! A messenger has been sent from Lu'ayy ibn Ghalib.' Then it began to recite:

I marvelled at the jinn and their pursuit, and their driving of camels with their saddle-cloths.
They yearn towards Makkah seeking guidance; the best of the jinn are not like their wretched ones.
So rise to the chosen one of Hashim, and let your eyes be turned towards its head.

He said: Then it roused me and frightened me and said: 'O Sawad ibn Qarib! Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has sent a prophet, so rise towards him and you will be guided and rightly directed.' When it was the second night, it came to me, roused me, and then began to recite:

I marvelled at the jinn and their pursuit, and their driving of camels by their saddle-pads.
They yearn towards Makkah seeking guidance; their two forefeet are not like their tails.
So rise to the chosen one of Hashim, and let your eyes be turned towards its [forehead].

When it was the third night, it came to me, roused me, and then said:

I marvelled at the jinn and their knowledge [of the unseen], and their driving of camels by their packs.
They yearn towards Makkah seeking guidance; those with evil are not like the good among them.
So rise to the chosen one of Hashim; the believing jinn are not like their unbelievers.

[p. 5363] He said: When he heard it repeated night after night, the love of Islam entered my heart, by the decree of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to the extent that Allah willed. He said: I went to my saddlebag, tied it tightly on my mount, and did not untie one cord or tie another until I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He was in Madinah, meaning Makkah, and the people around him were like the mane of a horse. When the Prophet ﷺ saw me, he said: "Welcome to you, O Sawad ibn Qarib. We know what has brought you." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have composed a poem. Let me recite it to you." He ﷺ said: "Say it, O Sawad." So I said:

My companion came to me after a night and a sleep,
and in what I have tested, he was never a liar.

Three nights, each night he would say:
"A messenger from Luayy ibn Ghalib has come to you."

So I hitched up my izar above my calves,
and the swift, strong she-camel carried me through the desert plains.

I bear witness that Allah, there is no lord but Him,
and that you are trusted over every unseen matter.

And that you are the nearest of the messengers in intercession
to Allah, O son of the most noble and the best.

So command us with what comes to you, O best of messengers,
even if what has come is the greying of the forelocks.

Be for me an intercessor on the day when no one has intercession
besides you, to suffice for Sawad ibn Qarib.

He said: The Prophet ﷺ laughed until his back teeth were visible, and said to me: "You have prospered, O Sawad!" Then Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: "Does your companion still come to you now?" He said: "Since I recited the Qur'an, he has not come to me, and the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is a fine replacement for the jinn." Then al-Bayhaqi transmitted it through two other routes. The words of Ibn Kathir end here.

It has been related by Imam al-Mawardi in (A'lam al-Nubuwwah) together with similar reports, in the sixteenth chapter, on the calls of the jinn. Then he said: Even if these calls are khabar al-ahad (solitary reports) from one whose person is not seen and whose testimony is not decisive, their departure from the ordinary habit is a warning, and their effect on souls is a glad tiding, and the listeners have accepted them. The acceptance of reports confirms their soundness and supports their proof. If it is said: If the calls of the jinn are among the signs of prophethood, [p. 5364] then it could also be a proof for the validity of kahanah (soothsaying), then there are two answers to this:

The first: the signs of prophethood are other than these; rather, these are among its heralds, and he distinguished between a sign (dalalah) and a glad tiding (bisharah) by way of information.

The second: soothsaying concerns the hidden, while glad tidings concern a specific matter; the observed is known, and the unseen is imagined. The words of al-Mawardi end here.

The second point of caution:

Al-Mawardi said: Regarding the turning away (sarf) of the jinn mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: they were turned away from eavesdropping on the heaven by the hurling of shooting stars, and they were not turned away from it after Jesus except after the sending of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So they said: "This event in the heaven is only for an event on the earth," and they imagined in it the renewal of prophethood. So they traversed the earth until they came upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the valley of Makkah, as he was heading to Ukaz and was performing the dawn prayer. They listened to the Qur'an, saw how he prayed, and his companions followed him. Thus they knew that this was for this event, and they were turned away from eavesdropping by the hurling of meteors. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.

I say: According to this view, the (ila) in (ilayka) means the same as the lam of causation. It is mentioned in (al-Mughni) that it may come synonymous with the lam, as in: "and the matter is to you." But this is strained and remote, because it is far from what the context of the rest of the verse requires.

Then al-Mawardi said: [p. 5365] Ikrimah related that the surah he used to recite was ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-Alaq: 1]. I say: It will come later, traced back to the Prophet through Jabir, that it was Surat al-Rahman.

Then al-Mawardi said:

The second interpretation: they were turned away from their lands by divine guidance, through Allah's grace, until they came to the Prophet of Allah in the valley of Nakhlah. Then Jibril descended to him with this verse, informed him of the coming of the jinn, and commanded him to go out to them. He went out with Ibn Masud, until he came to al-Hajun. Ibn Masud said: "He drew a line for me and said: Do not cross it."

According to the first interpretation, he did not know of them until they came to him. According to the second interpretation, Jibril informed him before their coming. The scholars differed over whether he saw them and recited to them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not see them and did not recite to them; rather, they heard his recitation when they passed by him while he was praying. Ibn Masud related that he saw them and recited the Qur'an to them.

I say: What Ibn Kathir has mentioned earlier is sufficient.

Then al-Mawardi said: Regarding His saying ﴿When they attended it, they said: Be silent﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: when they attended his recitation of the Qur'an, they said: "Be silent to listen to it."

The second: when they attended the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they said: "Be silent to listen to his words." The words of al-Mawardi end here.

Ibn Kathir said: This, that is their saying "Be silent," is a mark of good manners on their part. Al-Bayhaqi related from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Surat al-Rahman until he finished it, then said: 'Why do I see you silent? The jinn were better than you in response. Every time I recited to them this verse: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾, they would say: "Nor do we deny any of Your favours, our Lord; to You be praise."'" It was also transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, who said: "We do not know it except from the hadith of al-Walid ibn Muslim from Zuhayr."

The third point: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31] indicates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent generally to both mankind and the jinn.

[p. 5366] Ibn Kathir said: Because he called the jinn to Allah, and recited to them the surah in which there is address to both groups, their obligations, promises, and threats, and that is Surat al-Rahman. This is why He said: ﴿Respond to the caller of Allah and believe in Him﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. Al-Mawardi said: The scholars have not disagreed that it is permissible for Allah to send a messenger from mankind to them, but they differed over the permissibility of a messenger from among them. Some permitted it, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130], while others forbade it. This is the view of those who made them the offspring of Iblis, and they interpreted His saying ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130] as referring to those who, when they heard the Qur'an, turned back to their people as warners. The words of al-Mawardi end here.

I say: A parallel to this is the naming of the messengers of Jesus, peace be upon him, as "messengers" in the verse ﴿When We sent to them two﴾ [Ya-Sin: 14].

The fourth point: Those scholars who held that believing jinn do not enter Paradise have used as evidence His saying ﴿He will forgive you of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. They said: the reward of their righteous ones is only that they be protected from the punishment of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection; for if they had a reward for faith higher than this, it would have been mentioned.

Al-Mawardi said: As for their disbelievers, they will enter the Fire. As for their believers, they differed over whether they enter Paradise as a reward for their faith. Al-Dahhak said: "Whoever permits that their messengers were from among them, they will enter Paradise." Sufyan related from Layth that they will be rewarded for faith by being protected from the Fire, and then it will be said to them: "Be dust like the beasts." The words of al-Mawardi end here.

The truth, as Ibn Kathir said, is that their believer is like the believer among mankind; they enter Paradise, as is the view of a group of the early generations (al-salaf). Some of them have used as evidence for this His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾ [al-Rahman: 74]. But there is room for scrutiny in this argument. A better proof is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 47]. He, the Exalted, has bestowed His favour upon both the two weighty groups by making the reward of their good-doers Paradise. The jinn responded to this verse with verbal gratitude more eloquently than mankind, saying: "Nor do we deny any of Your favours, our Lord; to You be praise." So He, the Exalted, would not bestow favour upon them with a reward that they do not attain.

Also, if He repays their disbelievers with the Fire, which is a station of justice, then all the more He repays their believers with Paradise, which is a station of grace, by way of a stronger and more fitting argument. Among what also indicates the generality of this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging﴾ [al-Kahf: 107], and what resembles that of verses. What they have mentioned here of reward for faith, namely the expiation of sins and protection from the painful punishment, necessarily entails entering Paradise, because in the Hereafter there is nothing but Paradise or the Fire. Whoever is protected from the Fire enters Paradise without doubt. No explicit text or apparent evidence from the Lawgiver has reached us stating that believing jinn do not enter Paradise even if they are protected from the Fire; and if it were authentic, we would adopt it. And Allah knows best. Here is Noah, peace be upon him, saying to his people: ﴿He will forgive you of your sins and delay you until a specified term﴾ [Nuh: 4]. There is no disagreement that the believers among his people are in Paradise; so likewise these. Strange views have been reported about them. From Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: they will not enter the center of Paradise, but will be around its outskirts, its surroundings, and its edges.

Some people claimed that in Paradise the children of Adam will see them, while they will not see the children of Adam, the reverse of their state in the worldly abode. Some people said: they do not eat or drink in Paradise, but they are inspired with glorification, praise, and sanctification in place of food and drink, like the angels, because they are of their kind. All these views are open to scrutiny and have no proof. The words of al-Mawardi end here.

The fifth point: It has been said: the secret of the partial (tab'id) in His saying ﴿of your sins﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31] is that there is a punishment that is not forgiven by faith, such as the sins of injustice (al-mazalim), that is, the rights of people. But there is room for scrutiny in this, because if a combatant (harbi) plunders protected property and sheds sanctified blood, and then his Islam is good, Islam erases the sin of what came before him without any problem. [p. 5368] It is said: He did not promise forgiveness to the disbeliever on condition of faith in the Book of Allah except in a partial form. The secret of this is that the station of the disbeliever is constriction (qabd), not expansion (bast), and therefore his hope is not expanded as it is in the case of the believer. This was related by al-Nasir.

The sixth point: Ibn Kathir said: In their claim to their people they combined encouragement and warning, and for this reason it had an effect on many of them, and they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in delegations, delegation after delegation, as has already been explained.

The seventh point: Al-Mawardi said: The jinn belong to the speaking, discerning world. They eat, marry, reproduce, and die. Their persons are veiled from sight, although they are distinguished by actions and traces; but Allah singles out whom He wills to see them. Mankind came to know them from the divine books and from what they imagined of their hidden traces.

Al-Qashani said: The jinn are earthly souls embodied in subtle bodies composed of subtle elements. The sages of Persia named them "the suspended forms." Because they are earthly, embodied in elemental bodies, and share this with mankind, both are called "the two weighty ones" (al-thaqalan). Just as it was possible for people to challenge with the Qur'an, it was possible for them too, and the reports of them from the verifiers and others are more than can be counted, and too clear to accept interpretation. The words of al-Qashani end here.

The discussion of the words of His saying, Exalted is He:

[33] ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and did not tire in their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, indeed He is Competent over all things.﴾

﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and did not tire in their creation, is able to give life to the dead?﴾ That is: by restoring the soul to the body after its separation from it, and bringing them out of their graves in the same state they were in before their death.

In Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) there is a subtle grammatical discussion (bahth nahwi) on the entry of the preposition bi (the particle "ba'") into ﴿bi-qadirin﴾ (ﷺ-less: "able"), which is original. It is mentioned in the sections on the addition of the particle ba' (ziyadat al-ba'), in the extended works of Arabic grammar (al-Arabiyyah).

﴿Yes, indeed He is Competent over all things﴾ That is: including the restoring of what has ceased to exist, even if the body and everything else has perished.

(p-5369) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[34–35] ﴿And the Day those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "Is this not the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ ﴿So be patient, as the steadfast of the messengers were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. It is as if, the Day they see what they are promised, they had not remained but an hour of a day. [This is] a notification. So will anyone be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35].

﴿And the Day those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire, "Is this not⁠—﴾ meaning: [the resurrection] after being brought back to life: ﴿the truth?" They will say, "Yes, by our Lord." He will say, "So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ ﴿So be patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: in conveying the message and [bearing] their denial and harm: ﴿as the steadfast of the messengers were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: those of them who were firm and earnest, for you are among them. ʿAzm (resolve) linguistically is like ʿazimah, that to which you have fixed your heart regarding a matter. ʿAzm also means strength for something and perseverance in it. What is meant here is those who strive hard and are earnest, or those who persevere in God's command regarding what He has entrusted to them and decreed and ordained for them. The general notion of earnestness, exertion, and patience is found in all the messengers, indeed in the prophets, peace be upon them, and in many of the friends of God. Therefore, the majority of exegetes held in this verse that they are all the messengers, and that "min" (of) is explicative (bayaniyyah) rather than partitive (tab'idiyyah), so every messenger is among the steadfast ones of resolve. If by it is meant a meaning specific to some of them, then its explanation must be given so that the reason for the specification becomes clear. The source of disagreement about their number leads to several opinions:

The first: they are all the messengers. The second: they are four: Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Muhammad. The third: they are five, adding Jesus, as it has been said:

*The steadfast of resolve: Noah, the Intimate Friend (Abraham) who is glorified, Moses, Jesus, and the Prophet Muhammad.*

The fourth: they are six, adding Aaron or David. The fifth: they are seven, adding Adam. The sixth: they are nine, adding Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. It may be increased or decreased.

(p-5370) The justification for the specification is that what is meant by them are those who have complete earnestness and exertion in calling to the truth, and in defending the sanctity of monotheism and the protection of the Sharia, to the extent that they endure what others cannot bear, from their inner and bodily afflictions and external circumstances, such as confronting all the people of their age, as was the case with Noah, or a tyrannical king of their era, and triumphing over him without worldly preparation, like Nimrod against Abraham, Goliath against David, and Pharaoh against Moses; for every Moses there is a Pharaoh, and for every Muhammad an Abu Jahl. And [they endure] trials with matters that humans cannot bear without a holy power and a divine soul, as happened to Job, peace be upon him. From here the veil of obscurity is lifted from the face of the specification; this is among what the secret of their blessings has revealed. This was conveyed by al-Shihab.

﴿And do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: do not hasten, by questioning your Lord, the punishment upon them, for it will certainly descend upon them, even if the matter becomes hard for you because of them. ﴿It is as if, the Day they see what they are promised﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: of God's punishment, His retribution, and His disgrace that will descend upon them in this world or in the Hereafter: ﴿they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: because it will make them forget the severity of the punishment that descends upon them, the measure of what they stayed and the extent of what they dwelt in the world.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿a notification﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], Ibn Jarir said: it has two aspects:

The first: its meaning is: "they did not remain but an hour of a day" [this is] a remaining of notification, meaning: this is a notification for them in the world until their term; then he omitted "that is a remaining," though it is intended in the speech, being sufficiently indicated by what was mentioned.

The second: its meaning is: this Qur'an and the reminder is a notification and sufficiency for them, if they reflect and take heed, so that they remember. End quote.

Al-Mahayimi pointed to another meaning, saying: it is not the right of messengers to seek haste; rather, their right is notification.

﴿So will anyone be destroyed﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: by God's punishment when He sends it according to justice and wisdom: ﴿except the defiantly disobedient people﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: those who opposed His command and went out of His obedience. We seek refuge in God from His wrath and His painful punishment.

The first: they are all the messengers. The second: they are four: Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Muhammad. The third: they are five, adding Jesus, as it has been said:

*The steadfast of resolve: Noah, the Intimate Friend (Abraham) who is glorified, Moses, Jesus, and the Prophet Muhammad.*

The fourth: they are six, adding Aaron or David. The fifth: they are seven, adding Adam. The sixth: they are nine, adding Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. It may be increased or decreased.

(p-5370) The justification for the specification is that what is meant by them are those who have complete earnestness and exertion in calling to the truth, and in defending the sanctity of monotheism and the protection of the Sharia, to the extent that they endure what others cannot bear, from their inner and bodily afflictions and external circumstances, such as confronting all the people of their age, as was the case with Noah, or a tyrannical king of their era, and triumphing over him without worldly preparation, like Nimrod against Abraham, Goliath against David, and Pharaoh against Moses; for every Moses there is a Pharaoh, and for every Muhammad an Abu Jahl. And [they endure] trials with matters that humans cannot bear without a holy power and a divine soul, as happened to Job, peace be upon him. From here the veil of obscurity is lifted from the face of the specification; this is among what the secret of their blessings has revealed. This was conveyed by al-Shihab.

﴿And do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: do not hasten, by questioning your Lord, the punishment upon them, for it will certainly descend upon them, even if the matter becomes hard for you because of them. ﴿It is as if, the Day they see what they are promised﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: of God's punishment, His retribution, and His disgrace that will descend upon them in this world or in the Hereafter: ﴿they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: because it will make them forget the severity of the punishment that descends upon them, the measure of what they stayed and the extent of what they dwelt in the world.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿a notification﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], Ibn Jarir said: it has two aspects:

The first: its meaning is: "they did not remain but an hour of a day" [this is] a remaining of notification, meaning: this is a notification for them in the world until their term; then he omitted "that is a remaining," though it is intended in the speech, being sufficiently indicated by what was mentioned.

The second: its meaning is: this Qur'an and the reminder is a notification and sufficiency for them, if they reflect and take heed, so that they remember. End quote.

Al-Mahayimi pointed to another meaning, saying: it is not the right of messengers to seek haste; rather, their right is notification.

﴿So will anyone be destroyed﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: by God's punishment when He sends it according to justice and wisdom: ﴿except the defiantly disobedient people﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: those who opposed His command and went out of His obedience. We seek refuge in God from His wrath and His painful punishment.
